Count the 1 bits in the binary form of a number, without a built-in bit count.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/eliuds-eggs) (MIT). Listed under [Numbers & Math](/examples/?subject=numbers-and-math).

```nomi-run
// FILE: eliuds_eggs.nomi
//# Counts the eggs in Eliud's coop from the number its display shows.

/// Counts the 1 bits in the binary form of a non-negative `number`: the
/// eggs in Eliud's coop, one bit per nest.
pub fn egg_count(number: Int) -> Int {
    Iter.iterate(number, &(&1 >>> 1))
    |> Iter.take_while(&(&1 > 0))
    |> Iter.map(&(&1 &&& 1))
    |> Iter.sum()
}

// FILE: eliuds_eggs_test.nomi
import eliuds_eggs

test "counts the eggs" {
    cases = [
        #("0 eggs", 0, 0),
        #("1 egg", 16, 1),
        #("4 eggs", 89, 4),
        #("13 eggs", 2000000000, 13),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, number, expected), description {
        assert eliuds_eggs.egg_count(number) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The number is shifted right one bit at a time with `Iter.iterate(number, &(&1 >>> 1))`, cut at zero, and each step's low bit, `&(&1 &&& 1)`, is summed. Every stage is one operator, so each is a capture.
- The exercise forbids a built-in bit count, so the solution does not call `Int.bit_count(number)`, which answers the same.
- A negative number counts as 0 eggs, since the chain stops before its first step. The exercise only has non-negative inputs.
- The four cases are one `subtests` table.
